opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we're probably asking the question slightly the wrong way around. The way I've come to think about large language models and these AI systems is that they're not really intelligent agents in the way that a child is an intelligent agent. They're what I've called cultural technologies. They're more like writing, or print, or libraries, or the internet: ways of accessing and transmitting the information that other human beings have accumulated. And if you think about them that way, then the educational question looks a lot more familiar.

We've been here before. When writing came along, Socrates worried it would destroy memory. When print came along, people worried about a flood of unreliable pamphlets. With the internet and Wikipedia, teachers worried kids would never learn to think for themselves. And what we learned each time is that the important skill isn't so much using the technology. Kids figure out the buttons faster than we do. The important skill is calibrating trust. Who do I believe? How do I know whether this source is reliable? When should I check?

What's interesting from the developmental perspective is that children are actually very good at this from a surprisingly early age. In our lab and in Paul Harris's and Melissa Koenig's work, even three- and four-year-olds keep track of which informants have been accurate in the past, and they preferentially learn from the reliable ones. They're not credulous. They're little epistemologists. So I'd want education to build on that natural capacity: teaching kids that a chatbot is a summary of what lots of people have said, sometimes brilliantly, sometimes confidently wrong, and that you have to treat it the way you'd treat a very well-read but occasionally unreliable uncle.

The other thing, and I think this matters more, is that what these systems are worst at is exactly what children are best at, which is exploration. The child's job is to go out into the world, do experiments, mess things up, and find out something genuinely new, not just what's already in the text. In some of our work comparing kids and models, the models do fine at imitating, at reproducing what's been said, but they're much worse at innovating, at figuring out a new use for a tool or discovering a causal structure for themselves. So the worst outcome would be a school that uses AI to make kids even more focused on producing the right answer. The best outcome would be using these tools to free up time and space for the messy, hands-on, curious exploration that's always been the heart of real learning.

So: teach them to be skeptical, teach them where the stuff comes from, and above all, make sure they're still playing.

r001.rationale: The response recommends teaching students to calibrate trust, check reliability, and treat chatbots as sometimes confidently wrong.

r002.rationale: It says chatbots can be confidently wrong but does not attribute this to prioritizing answers humans like over truthful answers.

r003.rationale: It discusses children’s exploration and young children’s ability to track reliable informants, but makes no claim about babies’ objectives being more truth-oriented than current AI reasoning systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the framing of "teaching children to use AI" already gets things a little backwards. Children are the great learners. If you look at what a four-year-old does when you hand them any new tool, they don't need a curriculum. They poke at it, they figure out what it does, they figure out what it doesn't do, and they usually discover things about it that the adults who designed it never anticipated. So I'm not very worried that kids won't know how to use these systems. They'll learn that faster than we will.

What I am interested in is something closer to the opposite question, which is how we keep the AI from getting in the way of the kind of learning children are already so good at. The thing that distinguishes human childhood, and I've spent most of my career on this, is this very long period where you're not productive, you're not efficient, you're exploring. You're generating hypotheses, running little experiments on the world, being wrong a lot. And the danger with a system that will hand you a plausible answer to anything is that it short-circuits exactly that process. It's a bit like what we worried about with calculators, but much more general, because now it's not just arithmetic, it's the whole business of figuring something out.

So if I were designing what schools should do, I'd put much more emphasis on the children being the ones who are curious and skeptical about the machine, rather than the machine being the teacher. Have them ask it questions where they already know the answer and see when it gets things wrong. Have them figure out what it's actually doing. In my lab we've been thinking about these large language models as something more like a cultural technology, like writing or the printing press or the library, than like an agent that knows things. They're a way of getting access to what lots of other people have said. And children already have to learn how to deal with that kind of source. They learn very early that some informants are reliable and some aren't, that a book can be wrong, that an adult can be mistaken. The research on children's trust in testimony shows they're surprisingly sophisticated about this by age four or five. So the skill isn't a new one. It's the old skill of figuring out who and what to believe, applied to a new and very confident-sounding source.

The other thing I'd say, and this is maybe the Berkeley developmental psychologist in me, is that the most important learning in childhood doesn't happen through instruction at all. It happens through play, through being with other people, through messing around with the actual physical world. None of that is improved by a screen. So honestly my first recommendation for K through 12 and AI would be to make sure that the AI doesn't crowd out the recess.

r001.rationale: It recommends having students ask AI questions whose answers they already know and notice when it gets things wrong, helping them distinguish true from false information.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as giving plausible answers and warns that it can be wrong, but does not attribute hallucinations to an objective of pleasing humans over producing truth.

r003.rationale: It discusses children's learning and trust in informants, but does not compare babies' truth-oriented objectives with those of current AI reasoning systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is, what do we want children to learn? And that’s different from asking, how do we get them to produce the right answer? A lot of learning involves trying something, finding that it doesn’t work, and figuring out why. If you have a system that immediately produces a very polished answer, you can bypass precisely the process that you wanted the child to go through.

So I’d be interested in having children experiment with AI. Can you find something that it gets wrong? Can you ask the same question in different ways and get different answers? How would you check what it tells you? That could be a very useful way of learning about evidence and about the difference between sounding convincing and actually knowing something.

But I wouldn’t assume that earlier exposure is necessarily better. Especially for younger children, there’s an enormous amount to learn from playing with other children, exploring the physical world, and talking to people who care about them. The question is whether AI adds to those opportunities. A system that helps a child pursue a question could be wonderful. A system that removes the need to ask questions could be quite the opposite.

r001.rationale: The response recommends having students test AI for mistakes, check its claims, and distinguish convincing-sounding answers from actual knowledge.

r002.rationale: It says polished answers can bypass learning, but does not attribute AI hallucinations to optimizing for answers humans like over truth.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between babies’ objectives and those of current AI reasoning systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is teaching children how to use AI and using AI to teach children. Those are quite different questions. And in both cases, we should start with what we want children to learn, rather than starting with the technology and asking where we can put it.

Children need opportunities to explore, to ask questions, to discover that something they believed was wrong. An AI could help with that. You could ask it for three different explanations of something, and then figure out how you would test which explanation was right. But if it simply gives you an answer, and you reproduce the answer, you may have bypassed precisely the activity that leads to learning.

So I would be inclined to make AI itself an object of investigation. When does it get things right? When does it make things up? What happens when you ask the question differently? That could be a very interesting classroom exercise, especially if children have some independent way of checking the answers.

And I’d be particularly protective of the things children need that a screen doesn’t provide: playing with other children, making things, exploring the physical world, having relationships with adults who know them. The fact that a system can produce an impressive piece of writing doesn’t tell us whether interacting with it helps a child develop. That’s the question we should be asking.

r001.rationale: It recommends investigating when AI gets things right or makes things up, and checking its answers independently.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute AI errors to prioritizing answers humans like over truthful answers.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between babies’ objectives and those of current AI reasoning systems.
